articles.summary: The seniors housing and care sector entered 2026 with meaningful momentum, and the first half of the year suggests the industry is on track for one of its strongest transaction environments in recent memory. Rising occupancy, limited new supply, and growing investor confidence have combined to create favorable conditions for acquisitions, recapitalizations and portfolio repositioning across both seniors housing and skilled nursing. The market's resilience is particularly notable given a higher interest-rate environment that has challenged transaction activity across many commercial real estate sectors. While financing costs remain elevated, investors continue to pursue opportunities in seniors housing and care, supported by improving property-level performance and long-term demographic tailwinds. Seniors Housing Transaction Activity Reaches Record Pace Investment activity in seniors housing accelerated significantly during the first six months of 2026. More than 300 transactions closed domestically during the period, representing an increase of more than 40% compared with the first half of 2025. Based on current trends, annual transaction volume is projected to exceed 2025 levels by nearly 20%. A highly competitive bidding environment continues to drive activity. Average cap rates compressed to approximately 7.2% and average pricing exceeded $250,000 per unit during the second quarter. Notably, nearly one-quarter of reported transactions were priced above $300,000 per unit, highlighting investor willingness to pay premiums for desirable assets. Several factors are contributing to this momentum. Occupancy gains and margin expansion are helping operators achieve stabilization sooner than anticipated, creating greater flexibility around dispositions and generating a new wave of investment opportunities. At the same time, limited new development continues to constrain supply, reinforcing the value of existing properties. Investor interest remains especially strong in Florida, Texas and California, though competition for assets in those markets is increasingly pushing buyers into secondary and tertiary locations. Colorado emerged as one of the fastest-growing markets for investor interest during the first half of the year, illustrating the expanding search for opportunities beyond traditional destinations. Industry leaders are also expressing confidence in the sector's outlook. Executives highlighted ongoing acquisition efforts, a focus on building operating density and an expectation that limited development will leave demand growth outpacing new supply for years to come. Many are concentrating on acquiring existing assets rather than pursuing ground-up development, citing the time and complexity involved in delivering new communities. Demographics Continue to Support Long-Term Growth Even as transaction activity reaches new highs, investors remain focused on the long-term fundamentals driving the sector. The aging U.S. population, coupled with a prolonged period of underdevelopment, continues to create a compelling investment backdrop. Many operators and investors view today's supply constraints not as a short-term challenge but as a catalyst for sustained demand growth in the years ahead. In addition, operators are investing in renovations, technology enhancements and operational improvements to better align existing communities with evolving resident expectations. These initiatives are helping support revenue growth and improve asset competitiveness while avoiding the lengthy entitlement and construction timelines associated with new development. Public market performance further reflects growing confidence in the sector. Seniors housing providers benefited from improving occupancy trends, easing labor, and favorable demographic dynamics during the first half of 2026, contributing to stronger valuations and share-price performance among several publicly traded companies. Skilled Nursing Investment Activity Accelerates Momentum is not limited to seniors housing. Skilled nursing transaction volume also increased substantially during the first half of 2026. Nearly 140 skilled nursing transactions closed during the period, an increase of more than 30% compared with the second half of 2025. Current trends point to annual transaction volume exceeding 2025 levels by more than 25%. While owner-operators remained the dominant acquirers, accounting for nearly three-quarters of transaction activity, private equity firms, investment firms and REITs remained highly active participants. Many investors were attracted by improving operational performance, favorable reimbursement environments, and the opportunity to acquire assets at yields that compare favorably with other real estate sectors. Average skilled nursing cap rates remained near 11.5% during the first half of the year, while average pricing climbed approximately 25% compared with late 2025 levels. Occupancy approached decade highs, allowing operators to become more selective regarding payer mix and strengthening confidence in future operating performance. Industry executives also emphasized disciplined growth strategies, with many prioritizing acquisitions in existing markets and focusing heavily on operator quality. As one executive noted, the success of any transaction ultimately depends on the strength of the operating platform behind it. Looking Ahead While interest rates remain elevated and capital markets continue to evolve, the seniors housing and skilled nursing sectors appear well positioned for continued investment activity. Strong occupancy, limited supply, improving profitability and favorable demographics support both transaction volume and asset values. For investors, operators and capital providers, the theme emerging from the first half of 2026 is clear: operational fundamentals have strengthened significantly, and the capital markets are increasingly responding. As a result, seniors housing and skilled nursing appear poised to remain among the most active and closely watched sectors in commercial real estate for some time.
articles.title: Seniors Housing and Care Investment Activity Builds Momentum

articles.summary: Globe-Miami Resilience Fund Targets Flood Mitigation mboyle Thu, 10/29/2026 - 07:52 Post Image October 29, 2026 - The Globe-Miami Resilience Fund is making its first investment, committing approximately $250,000 to support development of a regional flood mitigation plan following devastating flooding last year. The plan is a collaborative effort involving Gila County, the Town of Miami and the City of Globe to identify ways to reduce future flood risks and strengthen the region's long-term resilience. The fund was established for the Globe-Miami community to reinvest the proceeds from a federal tax credit associated with the Miami smelter. Established by Freeport to support Arizona’s Globe-Miami area, the fund is expected to provide nearly $2 million in community investments. No additional funding has been allocated specifically to flood mitigation at this time. “Making communities stronger starts with understanding the people who live there,” said Robin Bradford, Social Performance Manager-Miami. “The Globe-Miami Resilience Fund was created to help turn that understanding into action, supporting projects that address local needs and continuing a legacy of responding to community priorities.” Determining those community priorities can happen through many forms, including resident surveys, stakeholder engagement and broader planning efforts. In the case of this mitigation effort, they stem from a shared experience. In 2025, severe flooding damaged homes, businesses and infrastructure throughout the area, prompting an extensive recovery effort. Following the event, Freeport contributed personnel and equipment to help the local community clear mud and debris from affected neighborhoods. While those efforts focused on immediate response and recovery, the regional flood mitigation plan is intended to help address the risk of future incidents. Funding from Freeport will support the engagement of an experienced public-sector post-wildfire flood mitigation expert, who will work alongside local public works, emergency management personnel and technical specialists to develop a comprehensive, long-term plan. The effort is expected to take at least two years. The resulting plan will include recommended mitigation measures, cost estimates, an education and communications plan, and a funding and financing plan to support future implementation. Local governments will work collaboratively to promote adoption of the plan and pursue funding to implement its recommendations. Bradford said this effort reflects the site’s significant and longstanding ties to the area and its commitment to helping build a better future for its residents. “As a company deeply rooted in the Globe-Miami area, we recognize both our responsibility and our opportunity to help lead solutions for the long term,” Bradford said. “By uniting local leadership, technical expertise, and a shared commitment to recovery, we’re helping turn a significant regional challenge into an opportunity to build a safer, more resilient future for the communities we call home.” Photo: Freeport provided volunteers, equipment and financial assistance to the Globe-Miami area following a 2025 flood.

articles.summary: 3D Systems Donates NextDent 300 3D Printer to Remote Area Medical to Expand Access to Free Denture Care in the U.S. Elizabeth Piet Thu, 10/29/2026 - 15:34 Release Date Thursday, Oct 29, 2026 3:34 PM Donation supports Remote Area Medical’s mission to bring high-quality dental care to underserved communities through advanced 3D printing technology. ROCK HILL, S.C., October 29, 2026 — 3D Systems (NYSE: DDD) today announced the donation of a NextDent® 300 MultiJet 3D printer to Remote Area Medical (RAM®), a nonprofit organization dedicated to providing free, quality dental, vision, and medical care to underserved and uninsured individuals in the United States. The donation supports RAM’s mission to eliminate barriers to essential healthcare by expanding its ability to provide customized, high-quality dentures to patients in need, at no cost. For individuals without access to affordable dental care, missing teeth can significantly affect their ability to eat, speak, and engage confidently in everyday life. Yet the cost of restorative dental treatment, including dentures, can place these essential services out of reach. Since 1985, RAM has worked to eliminate these barriers, delivering free healthcare services to more than one million patients across the United States. In 2025 alone, the organization served 32,770 patients and provided more than $16.6 million in free healthcare through the efforts of over 17,000 volunteers. After learning about RAM’s mission and its use of 3D Systems’ NextDent 5100 platform to provide dentures for underserved patients, 3D Systems CEO Jeff Graves saw an opportunity to further support RAM’s efforts. The donation of the Company’s new NextDent 300 MultiJet 3D printer will help RAM expand its digital denture manufacturing capabilities, enabling faster production of high-quality dentures for patients in need. The NextDent 300, powered by 3D Systems’ MultiJet 3D Printing technology, enables the production of highly realistic, durable monolithic dentures, with teeth and gums printed together as a single piece. By streamlining traditionally labor-intensive denture manufacturing processes, the solution helps reduce production time while delivering the precision, fit, and natural aesthetics patients deserve. The donated printer system is now installed and operational at RAM’s facility in Knoxville, Tennessee, where the organization is already using the technology to produce dentures for members of the community. Once RAM’s newest mobile dental laboratory is completed, the NextDent 300 will be integrated into the mobile unit, expanding the organization’s ability to bring advanced digital denture production directly to underserved communities across the country. “Remote Area Medical has an extraordinary record of bringing essential healthcare to people who need it most,” said Jeff Graves, CEO of 3D Systems. “We are proud to support that work with the NextDent 300, which enables the production of high-quality monolithic dentures more efficiently. The ability to eat comfortably, speak clearly, and smile with confidence can have a profound impact on a person’s quality of life. We hope this donation helps RAM extend that impact to even more patients.” “A Mirror Moment lasts only a few seconds, but its impact lasts a lifetime. It’s the first time in years someone smiles without covering their mouth, with the confidence to apply for a job, share a meal with family, or simply laugh out loud. Remote Area Medical’s partnership with 3D Systems lets us give patients high-quality dentures, and with them, a moment many thought they’d never have again. Together, we’re proving what’s possible when innovation and compassion share the same goal, one Mirror Moment at a time,” said Connor Gibson, Dental Technology Manager, Remote Area Medical. RAM’s ongoing investment in mobile healthcare services reflects its commitment to reaching patients who face geographic, financial, or other obstacles to treatment. The addition of the NextDent 300 will further support that work, helping the organization’s dental teams provide essential restorative care through an increasingly efficient digital workflow. 3D Systems looks forward to continuing to support Remote Area Medical’s community outreach. For more information about 3D Systems’ NextDent Jetted Denture Solution, visit www.3dsystems.com . To learn more about Remote Area Medical and its mission to provide free healthcare to underserved communities, visit www.ramusa.org . About 3D Systems For 40 years Chuck Hull’s curiosity and desire to improve the way products were designed and manufactured gave birth to 3D printing, 3D Systems, and the additive manufacturing industry. Since then, that same spark continues to ignite the 3D Systems team as we work side-by-side with our customers to change the way industries innovate. As a full-service solutions partner, we deliver industry-leading 3D printing technologies, materials and software to high-value markets such as medical and dental; aerospace, space and defense; transportation and motorsports; data center infrastructure; and durable goods. Each application-specific solution is powered by the expertise and passion of our employees who endeavor to achieve our shared goal of Transforming Manufacturing for a Better Future. More information on the company is available at www.3dsystems.com . About Remote Area Medical Remote Area Medical (RAM®) is a nonprofit provider of free dental, vision, and medical services to underserved and uninsured individuals. Through its network of volunteers, pop-up clinics, and mobile healthcare units, RAM delivers essential care to individuals and communities in need, regardless of their ability to pay. articles.summary: For 2 years, I have created Blueprints using a screen reader. Like many blind users, I have become highly skilled at navigating complex applications, moving through pages, locating controls, and finding the information I need. It is simply part of how I work. When I first heard about creating a Blueprint through AI chat, I was skeptical. My initial reaction was that there was no way this approach would be easier. I assumed I would spend more time trying to understand what the AI was doing than actually building the Blueprint. I expected frustration. I expected confusion. Honestly, I assumed I would prefer the traditional approach. After building an entire Blueprint with AI, I changed my mind. More Than Just a Faster Way to Build One of the biggest differences between the traditional Blueprint experience and the AI-assisted experience was that the conversation became part of my learning process. In the traditional interface, I can complete tasks because I know where things are and how they work. However, the interface does not always explain why something should be configured a certain way. With AI, I could ask questions as I worked. If I was adding a step to a stage, I could ask why that step might be useful. If I was unsure about a particular configuration choice, I could ask for an explanation. The assistant didn't just perform actions. It helped me understand the reasoning behind them. I found myself wishing I had access to this type of guidance when I first started at Pega. I believe I would have learned the Blueprint process much faster because I would have understood the purpose behind the configuration decisions rather than simply following steps. The Learning Curve Was Real My experience was not immediately positive, initially, I was actually less efficient using AI. I had to learn how to interact with it. I needed to understand the pace of the conversation, how to ask questions effectively, and what kind of information the assistant needed from me. There were moments early on when I wanted to stop using AI and go back to creating the Blueprint manually because it felt faster. But something interesting happened as I gained experience. The more I used the assistant, the more natural the interaction became. I learned how to shape my requests, and the assistant became easier to predict. By the end of the testing, I felt that I was working more efficiently than I would have been manually. More importantly, I wasn't just completing tasks. I learned throughout the process. Why AI Was Different for Me as a Screen Reader User The greatest benefit was not speed. It was navigation. Traditional applications often require screen reader users to spend significant time moving around an interface, locating controls, finding the correct section, and keeping track of where they are on the page. Over years of using assistive technology, this becomes second nature, but it still requires effort. With AI, much of that effort disappeared. Instead of spending time searching for controls, I could remain focused on the conversation and ask the assistant to perform actions on my behalf. This fundamentally changed how I interacted with Blueprint. Rather than navigating to accomplish work, I could simply describe my intent. That may seem like a small difference, but for a screen reader user it can significantly reduce the cognitive effort involved in navigating a complex application. Another unexpected advantage was spelling. I have never been a particularly strong speller. When creating case types or entering names, the assistant frequently understood what I intended and corrected minor mistakes automatically. It may sound like a small feature, but it removed another source of friction from the process. Where the AI Assistant Fell Short The experience was not perfect. One of my biggest frustrations was the inability to duplicate workflows through AI. Since workflow duplication can already be performed manually within Blueprint, I expected the assistant to support the same capability. Instead, I found myself repeatedly trying to convince the AI to perform an action it could not do. I also encountered challenges when working with uploaded files. In one case, the only file available for testing was related to cars. When I attempted to add it to an existing case type, the AI refused because the file content did not match the case type. To complete my testing, I ultimately had to create a car-related case type simply so the assistant would accept the file. There were also times when the AI needed information that I did not realize was required. For example, when working in Workflow Details, I eventually learned that I needed to specify which case type I wanted to modify before asking certain questions. However, if I was new user, rather than waiting for me to discover what information was missing, the assistant should have proactively asked: "Which case type would you like to work with?" Small prompts like that could make the experience much more approachable for someone learning Blueprint for the first time. A Different Way of Thinking About Accessibility I have used JAWS for a long time, and historically I have preferred direct navigation. It is what I know. It is what I trust. What surprised me during this evaluation was realizing how quickly that preference is changing. The more I work with AI, the more comfortable I become relying on conversational interactions. That does not mean traditional accessibility is no longer important. Users still need access to the interface and the ability to navigate independently. But AI introduces a new interaction model that complements traditional accessibility rather than replacing it. For me, it often feels less like driving through the interface and more like collaborating with a knowledgeable assistant. Looking Ahead The experience also made me think about what AI could do next. I would love to be able to say "undo the last change" and have the system automatically reverse the most recent action. I would like AI to duplicate workflows, modify release planning information, and describe reports and charts in a meaningful text format. As a blind user, one of the most exciting ideas is having AI help navigate the application itself. Imagine being able to say, "Take me to Release Planning" or "Take me to the next step," and being moved directly to the area where work needs to happen. That would allow AI not only to perform tasks, but also to act as an intelligent guide through the Blueprint creation process. Final Thoughts When I started this evaluation, I expected to prefer the traditional Blueprint experience. By the time I finished, I would have chosen the AI-assisted approach. The reason is not simply efficiency. It is that the experience changed how I interacted with the application. The AI reduced navigation overhead, helped me learn as I worked, corrected small mistakes, and made the Blueprint process feel more conversational and approachable. For a blind user who has spent years navigating software through a screen reader, that is a significant shift. What began as an experiment in AI-assisted Blueprint creation ended up feeling like a glimpse into a different future for accessibility, one where understanding, navigation, and productivity can all happen through conversation.
